outline_section.section_title: Introduction to Filter Interpretation from Magnitude Response
outline_section.learning_goal: Use the low- and high-frequency ends of $|H(j\omega)|$ to decide whether a filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean magnitude-response plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with the low-frequency and high-frequency ends highlighted and a unity line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the low-vs-high gain comparison rule that classifies a magnitude response as low-pass, high-pass, or neither.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with one smooth magnitude-response curve and compare only its low-frequency and high-frequency gain; do not introduce phase, cutoff formulas, or time-domain impulse responses.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the magnitude response as a comparison between the low-frequency end and the high-frequency end of the curve.
Use the unity line $|H(j\omega)|=1$ as the reference for whether a band is passed or attenuated.
State the low-pass template: low-frequency gain is larger than high-frequency gain.
State the high-pass template: high-frequency gain is larger than low-frequency gain, and explain that any response that does not fit either end-behavior template is neither.
Preview that the next sections will read actual plots and classify them.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction centered on the end-to-end comparison rule. Do not add phase, cutoff values, or any algebra beyond the unity-line and low/high-end comparison.

prompt_blocks.text: This magnitude-response curve has a smaller gain at low frequency than at high frequency. Which filter class best fits?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The only cue that matters here is the ordering of the two ends. Since the high-frequency end is larger than the low-frequency end, the filter is high-pass.

images.lesson_core_move: Classify a filter's passband behavior from its magnitude response by comparing low- and high-frequency gain to decide whether the LTI system is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

images.image_description: A magnitude-response plot with horizontal axis labeled $\omega$ and vertical axis labeled $|H(j\omega)|$. The low-frequency end is clearly below the unity reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$, the high-frequency end is clearly above it, and the curve makes a smooth upward transition between the ends. Keep the plot uncluttered and omit any phase information or extra panels.

outline_section.section_title: Classifying a High-Pass Filter from Magnitude Response
outline_section.learning_goal: Classify a magnitude-response curve as high-pass when the high-frequency end sits higher than the low-frequency end.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A magnitude-response plot with the low-frequency end below 1 and the high-frequency end above 1, so the curve clearly passes high frequencies better than low frequencies.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make the high-frequency side visibly stronger than the low-frequency side. Avoid extra panels or phase information.

question_policy.practice_question_model: The displayed magnitude-response curve has a lower low-frequency gain than high-frequency gain. Which filter class best fits?
distractor_plan: Choose low-pass by reversing the end comparison.
Choose neither even though the ends support high-pass.
Choose band-pass or band-stop instead of the requested passband class.
Judge by the largest peak instead of the low/high ends.
Ignore the low-frequency attenuation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the displayed magnitude-response curve, decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the high-frequency gain is larger than the low-frequency gain, so the filter is high-pass.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This mirrors the previous section with the low/high comparison reversed.
solution_step_plan: Read the low-frequency and high-frequency ends of the plot.
Check that the high-frequency gain is larger than the low-frequency gain.
Use that end comparison to identify high-pass behavior.
State the classification in one sentence.
practice_variation_axes: low end clearly below 1 while high end is above 1
low end near 1 while high end is clearly larger
different transition widths between the ends
different absolute gain levels with the same ordering
responses with a mild or strong low-frequency roll-off

outline_section.handoff_notes: Keep the comparison anchored on the two ends of the curve. Do not turn the example into a general filter-design discussion.

images.image_description: A clean magnitude-response plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with the low- and high-frequency ends both around 0.6, clearly below the unity line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$, while the middle region rises above 1 into a hump. Keep the graph uncluttered and instructional so the student must compare the two ends.

image_slot.image_description: A clean magnitude-response plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with the low- and high-frequency ends both around 0.6, clearly below the unity line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$, while the middle region rises above 1 into a hump. Keep the graph uncluttered and instructional so the student must compare the two ends.

outline_section.section_title: Classifying Neither Low-Pass Nor High-Pass Behavior
outline_section.learning_goal: Reject low-pass and high-pass labels when the low- and high-frequency ends do not show a one-sided passband pattern.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A magnitude-response plot with low- and high-frequency ends at similar sub-unity gain and a central hump above 1, so the response is not low-pass or high-pass.
visual_elements: middle region that differs from the ends
single hump or notch that makes the response neither low-pass nor high-pass
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make the two ends look comparable so the student must reject both passband labels. Keep the middle feature obvious but secondary to the end comparison.

question_policy.practice_question_model: The displayed magnitude-response curve has low- and high-frequency ends at about the same gain, while the middle region rises differently. Which classification fits?
distractor_plan: Call it low-pass because one side looks stronger in the middle.
Call it high-pass because the curve rises somewhere on the plot.
Choose a band-pass or band-stop label instead of the requested passband classification.
Focus on the middle hump rather than the two ends.
Mistakenly treat similar low and high ends as evidence for low-pass or high-pass.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the displayed magnitude-response curve, decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the low- and high-frequency ends do not support either passband label, so the filter is neither low-pass nor high-pass.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the same end-comparison rule but uses a response whose ends do not separate into low-pass or high-pass behavior.
solution_step_plan: Read the low-frequency and high-frequency ends of the plot.
Notice that the ends are about the same height rather than showing a one-sided passage pattern.
Reject both low-pass and high-pass labels on that basis.
State that the correct classification is neither.
practice_variation_axes: low and high ends both below 1
low and high ends both above 1
a middle bump or notch that does not change the end comparison
responses that look like band-pass or band-stop shapes
different plateau levels with similar low and high ends

outline_section.handoff_notes: The point is to reject both passband labels using the low/high ends. The middle shape should support that conclusion, not replace it.

prompt_blocks.text: The displayed magnitude-response curve has low- and high-frequency ends at about the same gain, while the middle region rises differently. Which classification fits?
Use the two ends of the curve, not the middle hump, to decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low- and high-frequency ends are about the same height, so the curve does not show a one-sided passband pattern.
Since neither end is larger, the filter is neither low-pass nor high-pass.

Use the two ends of the curve, not the middle notch, to decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The low- and high-frequency ends sit at about the same gain, so the curve does not favor one side over the other.
That end comparison rules out both low-pass and high-pass, so the correct classification is neither.
